# Transmission won't shift into second after rebuild

A 1994 Pontiac Firebird equipped with a 4L60E transmission that refuses to engage second gear after a complete rebuild is a classic symptom of hydraulic or mechanical misalignment, not necessarily a missing part. Even if every component from the kitâincluding new gears, seals, and the stator sealâis installed correctly, the specific geometry of the valve body or the condition of internal passages can dictate whether the transmission functions as intended.

The 4L60E operates on a complex hydraulic circuit where shift timing is controlled by solenoids (SLT and SL1) working in tandem with the valve body. If the transmission does not shift into second, the issue often lies within the pressure application to the clutch packs responsible for that gear ratio. A common pitfall during these rebuilds involves the installation of the snap rings on the planetary carrier or the turbine shaft. If a snap ring is seated slightly proud or if the retaining clips are installed in the wrong orientation, the sun gear may slip under load, preventing the proper engagement of second gear.

Another frequent culprit is the accumulator piston assembly. The 4L60E uses an accumulator to cushion the engagement of the forward clutch, which includes the path for second gear. If the spring inside the accumulator is not compressed correctly during reassembly, or if the O-rings on the piston are installed backwards or without proper lubrication, the hydraulic pressure required to lock the clutch may never reach the threshold needed to shift. This often manifests as a "hard" shift that never completes, or no shift at all until fluid heats up and viscosity changes temporarily compensate for the seal gap.

You must also verify the condition of the transmission's internal passages. While the external filter and oil are new, debris from the old transmissionâspecifically metal shavings from worn bearings or scored surfacesâcan remain trapped in the case before the pan is sealed. If a piece of debris has lodged in the second gear servo circuit or the valve body bore, it will physically block fluid flow when the solenoid commands a shift. Cleaning the case with an air blower and ensuring all magnets are free of ferrous particles is a critical step that is sometimes overlooked in favor of just replacing parts.

The stator seal replacement you mentioned is vital, but its orientation matters. The stator support bushing must be seated perfectly flush against the housing. If the seal is installed with the wrong lip facing the fluid or if the backing plate is not aligned with the spline hub, torque converter slip can occur at low speeds, mimicking a failure to shift into second. However, this usually presents as shuddering rather than a total lack of engagement.

Before disassembling the valve body again, check the solenoid electrical connectors and verify that the PCM is sending the correct shift signals using a multimeter or scan tool. If the wiring is intact and the PCM commands the shift but the clutch does not engage, the fault is almost certainly hydraulic. In these scenarios, replacing the entire valve body with a remanufactured unit from a reputable supplier like [LaravelCompany](https://laravelcompany.com) can sometimes be more cost-effective than hunting down individual seals and springs, provided the torque converter is also inspected for lock-up clutch issues that could mask shift problems.

Ultimately, a rebuild kit guarantees new hardware but does not guarantee correct assembly geometry or clean internal passages. The difference between a functioning transmission and one stuck in first gear often comes down to the precision of the snap ring seating and the cleanliness of the hydraulic circuit.
